name: Liberalism in the United States
summary: The American liberal tradition rests on the founding's Lockean principles: equal natural rights, government by consent, constitutional limits, free speech and religion, and separation of church and state. From the Progressive Era and especially Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal, it added an active federal government that regulates business, supports organized labor, taxes progressively and provides social insurance, on the view that freedom also needs economic security. At its mid-century peak it joined this mixed economy with civil rights, Keynesian economic management, free trade and an anticommunist internationalism built around the UN and the Western alliance.
scope: The mainstream American liberal tradition of the New Deal and its heirs, as the defining sources describe it (the Miller Center essay on Truman's domestic affairs, the Alterman and Mattson history of American liberalism, the Stanford Magazine essay on modern American liberalism and Cold War liberalism): Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal and Second Bill of Rights, Truman's Fair Deal, Kennedy's liberalism and Johnson's Great Society. Answers rest on those presidents' own speeches and on the Declaration of Independence. It excludes libertarianism, American conservatism, the New Left and the contemporary Democratic program (modern-liberalism-in-the-united-states), whose later positions on abortion, LGBT rights, climate and gender this profile leaves null.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Truman stated that until a system of world security can be relied on, the country must maintain armed forces sufficient to deter aggression.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Declaration holds that all men are created equal, which leaves no place for rank by birth.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Truman proposed extending rent control and building low-rent public housing, which presumes rented homes will continue.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Roosevelt's Four Freedoms include the freedom of every person to worship God in his own way, which leaves no room for punishing leaving a religion.

ban-cartels.rationale: Truman proposed closing the loopholes that permit monopolistic mergers, and Roosevelt's 1944 list of rights includes freedom from domination by monopolies.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Truman said the country's progress confounded the gloomy prophets who predicted the downfall of American capitalism.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Truman criticized leaving disabled people to the mercy of charity and asked for expanded social security benefits.

class-collaboration.rationale: Roosevelt named class antagonism among the enemies of the country, and Truman asked for cooperation from farmers, labor and business.

clerical-rule.rationale: Kennedy rejected any prelate telling a President how to act and called America officially neither Catholic, Protestant nor Jewish.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Truman's 1949 message asks that the Wagner Act be reenacted and speaks of preserving free collective bargaining, while also proposing machinery to prevent strikes in vital industries.

collective-defense.rationale: Truman's inaugural proposed a North Atlantic collective defense arrangement to show the joint determination of free countries to resist armed attack from any quarter.

conscription.rationale: Truman's 1949 message says universal training is essential to the security of the United States.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Declaration of Independence says governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, and Johnson cited that phrase as a founding purpose.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: Roosevelt's 1944 chat lists trial by jury among the inalienable political rights under whose protection the republic began.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Johnson's Howard University speech says equal opportunity is not enough and that the task is equality as a fact and as a result, since ability is stunted by past conditions.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Roosevelt's 1944 chat names a right to a decent home, medical care, security in old age and unemployment, and a useful job, and asks Congress to implement them.

democracy-best.rationale: Truman's inaugural contrasts democracy, based on the conviction that people can govern themselves, with communism's rule by strong masters, and defends democracy as the right foundation.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Truman's inaugural rejected communism as a false philosophy of rule by strong masters, in favor of self-government.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Kennedy said the United States seeks to strengthen the United Nations and develop it into a genuine world security system able to resolve disputes on the basis of law.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Truman proposed the North Atlantic collective defense pact, saying every participating country must contribute all it can to the common defense.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Kennedy asks whether all Americans are to be afforded equal rights and equal opportunities, and Truman says no discrimination because of ancestry, religion, race or color is justifiable.

farm-price-support.rationale: Truman's 1949 message states that farm price supports are an essential part of the program, to prevent price declines out of line with general prices.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Truman proposed considering higher personal income rates in the middle and upper brackets, which assumes graduated rates rather than one flat rate.

nation-first.rationale: Truman called international cooperation the guiding star of foreign policy and a national commitment as profound as anything in history.

national-self-determination.rationale: Roosevelt cited the Atlantic Charter's self-determination of nations and peoples, and the Yalta statement affirmed the right of all peoples to choose their form of government.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Declaration states that all men are created equal and that just government rests on consent, which leaves no class of people born to rule.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Kennedy said he believes in a government which acts and exercises its full powers, and Truman's program rests on government work on health, housing, education and social security.

one-party-rule.rationale: Kennedy told the UN that systems which know only one party suppress free debate and free elections, and Truman called rule by strong masters a false philosophy.

party-controls-media.rationale: Kennedy criticized one-party systems that suppress free newspapers and free books.

positive-liberty.rationale: Roosevelt states that true individual freedom cannot exist without economic security and independence, and that people accepted a second Bill of Rights on that basis.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Roosevelt asked Congress to stabilize all farm prices, including food, to hold down the cost of living in wartime, and Truman sought standby price ceilings on scarce commodities.

price-controls-fight-inflation.rationale: Truman asked for standby authority to impose price ceilings on scarce commodities against inflation, and Roosevelt undertook to freeze the cost of living in 1942.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Truman's 1949 message says the country is doing what it can to encourage free states and free peoples throughout the world, and Kennedy pledged to support any friend to assure the success of liberty.

property-franchise.rationale: Johnson said every American citizen must have an equal right to vote, which excludes limiting the vote to property owners.

race-based-immigration-restrictions.rationale: Johnson's 1965 message called for an immigration law based on the work a man can do and not where he was born.

racial-franchise.rationale: Johnson told Congress that every American citizen must have an equal right to vote and that no reason can excuse its denial.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Kennedy asked Congress for a law giving all Americans the right to be served in public accommodations, calling its denial an arbitrary indignity.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Truman called the minimum wage far too low and asked that it be raised to at least 75 cents an hour, and Roosevelt's 1944 list of rights includes the right to earn enough to provide adequate food, clothing and recreation.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Truman asked for regulation of commodity speculation, control of bank credit and stronger antitrust laws, and Roosevelt named business and financial monopoly as an enemy.

rent-control.rationale: Truman asked Congress to extend and strengthen rent control in 1949.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Declaration says that when government becomes destructive of unalienable rights, the people have a right to alter or abolish it.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Roosevelt's Four Freedoms include the freedom of every person to worship God in his own way everywhere in the world.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Truman proposed banning jurisdictional strikes and unjustified secondary boycotts and machinery to prevent strikes in vital industries, yet vetoed Taft-Hartley as an abuse of workers' rights.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Kennedy told Yale graduates that political labels and ideological approaches are irrelevant to the solution of economic problems, which call for practical management.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Kennedy pledged to help the poor abroad because it is right, saying a society that cannot help the many who are poor cannot save the few who are rich, and Truman proposed a program for underdeveloped areas.

separate-church-state.rationale: Kennedy declared in 1960 that he believes in an America where the separation of church and state is absolute.

social-market-economy.rationale: Truman describes a private enterprise economy backed by social security expanded against the hazards of unemployment, old age, sickness and disability.

state-harmful.rationale: Kennedy called government an art and a precious obligation that should act when it has a job to do.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Truman proposed joining a collective defense pact of free countries against armed attack and promised military aid to free nations.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Kennedy criticized systems that suppress free debate, free elections and free trade unions.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Truman asked to extend social security coverage to the third of workers it excluded and to raise benefits, a universal program rather than one limited to the poorest.

total-state.rationale: Kennedy said he does not believe in a super state and does not favor state compulsion when voluntary effort can do the job.

unions-good.rationale: Truman's veto message calls the Taft-Hartley bill unfair to working people and an abuse of their right to join together and bargain, and Kennedy salutes the labor movement's struggle as part of the liberal cause.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Truman's 1949 message calls for a system of prepaid medical insurance that will enable every American to afford good medical care, and Roosevelt's 1944 Second Bill of Rights lists the right to adequate medical care.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Roosevelt called government by organized money as dangerous as government by an organized mob, and Truman rejected the theory that the nation's fortunes belong in a privileged few's hands.

notes: Second pass (2026-11-13) on the first pass's Wikipedia-based answers. Read: Miller Center speeches of Roosevelt, Truman, Kennedy and Johnson (searched by theme: economy, labor, civil rights, religion, government, war and alliances, trade, aid, taxes, health, housing, prices, immigration), Truman's 1949 Fair Deal message, Kennedy's 1960 Liberal Party speech. Each answer now rests on a passage in those speeches; answers the first pass drew from Wikipedia or general liberal theory, and positions that came only after the tradition's peak, are null. The speeches read do not show the classical and New Deal strands splitting on property and markets, so those statements are null, not 0. Books by Hamby, Matusow, Milkis and Mileur and Alterman and Mattson have no open full text; only the Publishers Weekly review of Alterman and Mattson was opened.
